title: CP asymmetry and visible decay in $3+1$ neutrino oscillations on a quantum computer
authors: Amartya Sengupta, Sidhartha Samtani, Ani Girgvliani, Dejan Stojkovic
abstract: We use quantum simulation to study how visible neutrino decay modifies the vacuum CP asymmetry in muon-to-electron oscillations within a $3+1$ neutrino scenario. The decay channel preserves CP symmetry, with CP violation arising from phases in the mixing matrix. We track the energy redistribution from visible decay and distinguish how parent attenuation and daughter regeneration modify the CP asymmetry. For the reference benchmark, the regenerated contribution is $4.85\times10^{-4}$, approximately $46\%$ of the total decay-induced shift. The full circuit for an effective two-energy model agrees with independent classical evolution. On an IBM quantum processor, we prepare the daughter state conditioned on decay and restore its physical normalization using fixed source and decay probabilities. After correction for measurement errors, the flavor-probability and coherence measurements both agree with the prediction within one standard error. Null controls test the suppression of the regenerated signal when daughter coherence or the relevant CP-sensitive mixing factor vanishes.
summary: This paper uses quantum simulation to model how neutrino decay affects the CP asymmetry in neutrino oscillations within a $3+1$ model. It separates the effect into parent attenuation and daughter regeneration, demonstrating that the quantum simulation results match classical predictions. This work is significant for understanding neutrino physics using quantum computing tools.
main_problem: The study investigates how visible neutrino decay modifies the vacuum CP asymmetry observed in muon-to-electron neutrino oscillations within a $3+1$ neutrino framework.
main_result: The quantum simulation results for both flavor-probability and coherence measurements agreed with theoretical predictions within one standard error, confirming the model's consistency.
method: The authors combine quantum simulation on an IBM quantum processor with theoretical modeling using open-system dynamics (Lindblad master equation) to track energy redistribution.
